title: Understanding the Beat-to-Beat Variations of P-Waves Morphologies in AF Patients During Sinus Rhythm: A Scoping Review of the Atrial Simulation Studies

subsections.subsection_title: Scoping Review Methodology and Organizational Framework
subsections.content:
This review was designed as a scoping review because the literature on beat-to-beat P-wave morphology variation in atrial fibrillation (AF) patients during sinus rhythm spans heterogeneous aims, methods, and evidence types, ranging from biophysical simulation studies to translational electrocardiographic phenotyping. Consistent with foundational scoping frameworks, the objective was to map the extent, nature, and conceptual organization of the field, identify knowledge gaps, and clarify how simulation studies have been used to interpret atrial electrical heterogeneity rather than to estimate pooled effects ref [1], ref [2].

Methodologically, we followed the iterative logic established for scoping studies, in which question refinement, search development, study selection, and data charting proceed recursively as familiarity with the evidence base increases ref [1], ref [2]. The review question was structured around population, concept, and context: AF-related atrial substrate and sinus-rhythm P-wave morphology; computational or simulation-based interrogation of atrial activation and conduction; and relevance to AF initiation, monitoring, or phenotyping. In keeping with scoping guidance, broad eligibility criteria were used to capture mechanistic simulation papers, image-based atrial models, electrophysiological modeling studies, and translational studies linking simulated atrial activation to surface ECG observables ref [2].

Searches should therefore be understood as comprehensive rather than effect-oriented, with emphasis on mapping published evidence and tracing conceptual linkages across modeling, signal analysis, and clinical interpretation ref [1], ref [2]. Study selection and charting were organized to extract model characteristics, substrate assumptions, atrial anatomy representation, rhythm condition, simulated biomarkers, and reported links to P-wave morphology variability. Results are reported descriptively and thematically, reflecting scoping-review practice in which formal risk-of-bias assessment and quantitative synthesis are typically not the primary aims ref [1], ref [2]. The remainder of this survey is organized accordingly: from clinical and pathophysiological context, to relevant signals and biomarkers, and finally to the role of computational modeling in explaining AF-related atrial electrical phenotypes.

subsections.subsection_title: Signals, Biomarkers, and Phenotyping Relevant to AF Initiation and Monitoring
subsections.content:
Signals used to phenotype atrial vulnerability during sinus rhythm span conventional ECG intervals, high-resolution P-wave morphology, and dynamic beat-to-beat descriptors. Among these, P-wave analysis is especially relevant because it encodes atrial depolarization pathways, interatrial conduction routes, and substrate heterogeneity that may precede overt arrhythmia. Contemporary reviews emphasize that duration alone is an incomplete surrogate: morphology, polarity, terminal force, and lead-dependent patterning can reveal local conduction disturbances even when global prolongation is modest ref [4]. This distinction is central for AF-oriented phenotyping, particularly in patients with paroxysmal disease or limited structural remodeling ref [4].

Beyond static templates, variability over time has emerged as a candidate biomarker of imminent AF initiation and of the remodeled atrial substrate. Martínez et al. showed that increased beat-to-beat variability in P-wave arc length and area during the hours preceding paroxysmal AF improves discrimination between healthy rhythm, remote pre-AF segments, and ECGs recorded close to AF onset, supporting the concept of progressive conduction instability before arrhythmia initiation ref [3]. Consistently, Censi et al. quantified cross-correlation-, amplitude-, and warping-based P-wave variability indices after cardioversion and found markedly greater variability in AF patients than in controls, with cross-correlation showing particularly high diagnostic performance ref [5]. Together, these studies motivate phenotyping frameworks that combine conventional duration/dispersion measures with morphology-derived variability metrics.

P-wave biomarkers are also relevant for longitudinal monitoring and treatment response. Reduction in P-wave duration after pulmonary vein isolation has been associated with successful lesion delivery and freedom from AF recurrence, suggesting that the terminal P-wave may partly reflect activation of pulmonary-vein sleeves and that post-ablation shortening can serve as a noninvasive procedural marker ref [6]. Accordingly, AF phenotyping for this review is organized around three signal layers: static morphology, beat-to-beat variability, and intervention-induced remodeling, each linking surface ECG observations to underlying atrial conduction mechanisms ref [4], ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Computational Modeling in AF Mechanisms and Translation
subsections.content:
Computational modeling has become a central mechanistic tool in AF research because it links cellular electrophysiology, atrial anatomy, fiber architecture, and substrate remodeling within a controllable in silico environment. Early morphologically realistic studies showed that discrete atrial structures—such as the crista terminalis, vena caval orifices, and coronary sinus musculature—shape reentry pathways and rotor anchoring, thereby clarifying why similar triggers may yield different macroscopic activation patterns in different substrates ref [12]. Species-specific platforms further established how regional ionic heterogeneity and conduction anisotropy create conditions for conduction block and rapid atrial arrhythmias, first in canine atria and later in sheep models that explicitly examined pulmonary-vein-driven AF initiation and maintenance ref [11], ref [8].

Beyond qualitative mechanism testing, contemporary models increasingly support translational questions. Reviews of virtual ablation studies emphasize that simulations are most informative when they explain why a lesion set succeeds or fails in a given substrate, rather than merely reproducing procedural endpoints ref [7]. Patient-specific workflows now combine imaging-derived anatomy, rule-based or mapped fiber orientation, electrophysiological personalization, and lesion representation to simulate radio-frequency ablation and to interpret post-procedural conduction gaps ref [10]. These frameworks have also shown that fibrosis distribution can determine where rotors stabilize, with slow conduction in patchy border zones promoting localized drivers and suggesting imaging-informed ablation targets ref [12].

For AF pathophysiology, modeling has been especially valuable in disentangling electrical remodeling from structural remodeling. Three-dimensional virtual human atria demonstrated that AF-induced ionic remodeling abbreviates action potential duration non-uniformly, amplifies vulnerability at key junctions such as CT/PM and PV/LA, and stabilizes faster reentrant activity ref [17]. Multiscale fibrosis models further indicate that myocyte-fibroblast coupling and reduced tissue conductivity can shift rotor dynamics from meandering wavelets to substrate-locked drivers in patient-specific fibrotic regions ref [12]. For the present review topic, these advances are highly relevant: they provide the mechanistic bridge from beat-to-beat atrial conduction variability during sinus rhythm to latent AF substrates that may already perturb activation pathways and, ultimately, P-wave morphology before overt arrhythmia emerges ref [10], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Context and Pathophysiological Basis of Atrial Fibrillation
subsections.content:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent sustained arrhythmia and a major cause of stroke, heart failure, hospitalization, and excess mortality, with lifetime risk rising markedly with age and comorbidity burden such as hypertension, valvular disease, obesity, diabetes, and sleep apnoea ref [14], ref [15], ref [16], ref [17]. Clinically, AF is classified as paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent, but these temporal patterns also reflect progressive substrate remodeling rather than merely episode duration ref [15], ref [16].

Mechanistically, AF emerges from the interaction between triggers and a vulnerable atrial substrate. The seminal observation that ectopic beats from the pulmonary veins can spontaneously initiate AF established focal firing as a key initiator, especially in paroxysmal disease ref [10]. Sustained AF then depends on re-entry promoted by shortened refractoriness, conduction heterogeneity, fibrosis, and autonomic imbalance; these concepts are synthesized in major pathophysiological reviews ref [14], ref [16], ref [18]. Experimental work further showed that “AF begets AF,” whereby rapid atrial activation induces electrical remodeling that stabilizes the arrhythmia and favors progression from intermittent to sustained forms ref [21].

For the present review, this clinical substrate is especially relevant because beat-to-beat P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm may encode latent atrial remodeling before overt AF recurrence. Left atrial enlargement has long been linked to AF risk ref [11], and contemporary evidence emphasizes structural, calcium-handling, and molecular abnormalities even in paroxysmal AF patients in sinus rhythm ref [13], ref [18]. Accordingly, sinus-rhythm atrial signals should be interpreted as markers of an underlying arrhythmogenic milieu rather than as purely normal electrical activity ref [14], ref [15], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Electrophysiological Mechanisms and Multiscale Atrial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Anatomical, Structural, and Multiscale Atrial Tissue Modeling
subsections.content:
Anatomical atrial modeling has evolved from idealized monolayers to image-based, structurally annotated geometries that explicitly represent chambers, venous ostia, appendages, septal structures, and major conduction bundles. Early MRI-derived human atrial models demonstrated that realistic chamber size and obstacle placement already shape wave break, reentry, and activation pathways, even when anisotropy is simplified ref [23], ref [17]. Subsequent whole-atrium reconstructions incorporated fiber orientation and torso coupling, enabling more faithful simulation of activation timing and the link between atrial sources and body-surface signals ref [12], ref [19].

A major advance for mechanistic studies was the explicit inclusion of structure-specific anisotropy and layered architecture. Fiber-informed human atrial models showed that regional bundle organization governs electrogram morphology and arrhythmic activation patterns ref [12]. Bilayer formulations further captured endo-epicardial dissociation, abrupt transmural fiber changes in the left atrium, and the discrete role of crista terminalis and pectinate muscles while remaining computationally tractable for long simulations ref [14]. Structure-specific reconstructions of the right atrial appendage and image-based sheep atria similarly emphasized that fine-scale bundle geometry and local myofiber organization critically modulate conduction, local activation delay, and vulnerability to reentry ref [16], ref [17], ref [22].

Multiscale tissue models increasingly integrate specialized nodal tissues and extracardiac volume conductors. A three-dimensional right atrial model including sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes reproduced classical nodal behaviors and highlighted how anatomical pathways, block zones, and anisotropy constrain propagation ref [11]. More recent detailed human atria–torso frameworks quantified how only selected atrial regions dominate the body-surface P-wave, reinforcing that beat-to-beat P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm depends not only on cellular electrophysiology but also on individualized atrial geometry, fiber architecture, wall layering, and interatrial connections ref [19].

subsections.section_title: Electrophysiological Mechanisms and Multiscale Atrial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Cellular Electrophysiology and Human Atrial Myocyte Models
subsections.content:
Human atrial myocyte modeling has progressed from early Hodgkin–Huxley–type formulations centered on repolarizing K+ currents to increasingly detailed representations of Ca2+ cycling, subcellular compartments, and disease remodeling. Foundational models by Nygren et al. and Courtemanche et al. established the basic human atrial AP framework and clarified how Ito/Isus/IKur, IKr, IKs, IK1, and ICaL interact to shape the marked heterogeneity of atrial repolarization and rate adaptation during sinus rhythm ref [33], ref [36]. These baseline formulations remain influential because they linked ionic current balance directly to AP morphology, refractoriness, and restitution properties relevant for atrial conduction and P-wave genesis ref [33], ref [36].

Subsequent generations of models addressed limitations in intracellular Ca2+ handling. Koivumäki et al. introduced spatially detailed SR release and uptake to reproduce the atrial-specific biphasic Ca2+ transient, delayed centripetal Ca2+ propagation, and the strong coupling between junctional Ca2+ release, NCX, and AP duration ref [30]. Grandi et al. further integrated human atrial AP and Ca2+ dynamics in sinus rhythm and chronic AF, highlighting how altered ICaL, IK1, IKs, INCX, SERCA, and SR leak reshape both repolarization and Ca2+ homeostasis under remodeling ref [37]. Maleckar et al. refined repolarizing K+ current formulations and rate dependence, whereas newer formulations explicitly account for variable T-tubule organization to interrogate structure–function coupling in AF-prone atrial cells ref [36], ref [35].

Comparative studies emphasize that no single atrial cell model is universally optimal. Benchmarking work has shown substantial divergence across published human atrial models in AP shape, long-term stability, alternans propensity, restitution, and tissue-level rotor behavior, underscoring the need to match model choice to the scientific question ref [34]. Likewise, patient-specific fitting studies demonstrated that both detailed and reduced-order atrial myocyte models can be tuned to reproduce individualized AP morphology and restitution, suggesting a practical route toward personalized multiscale simulations of sinus-rhythm substrates in AF patients ref [31]. Finally, in silico drug studies of AF-induced electrical remodeling identified atrial-selective targets such as IKur/Isus and highlighted how baseline ionic state determines whether a given intervention prolongs refractoriness or merely reshapes plateau voltage ref [15].

For a scoping review focused on beat-to-beat P-wave variability during sinus rhythm, these cellular models are indispensable because they define the ionic determinants of atrial excitability, recovery, and source–sink behavior that ultimately propagate upward to tissue activation timing and surface ECG morphology ref [31], ref [34], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Electrophysiological Mechanisms and Multiscale Atrial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Electrograms, Mapping, and Ablation in In Silico Atria
subsections.content:
In silico atrial models have become a crucial test bed for linking electrogram formation, mapping algorithms, and ablation response under controlled conditions. Simulation studies show that rotor and focal-source detection is highly sensitive to electrode configuration and sampling density: multi-electrode layouts alter apparent driver localization, and clinically relevant basket-like sparsity can introduce false phase singularities or miss meandering cores altogether ref [39], ref [41], ref [12]. These effects are compounded by signal modality, since unipolar and bipolar electrograms, interpolation, and preprocessing each reshape the inferred phase landscape and may transform relatively simple potential maps into apparently rotational patterns ref [41], ref [12]. Complementary entropy-based approaches likewise demonstrate that rotor-tip localization degrades as electrogram density decreases, with practical accuracy dropping once spacing exceeds roughly catheter-scale limits ref [45].

These methodological constraints have direct implications for interventional guidance. Catheter-navigation algorithms derived from simulated electrogram timing and first-activated bipoles can iteratively localize both rotor and focal sources without global panoramic coverage, illustrating how model-based signal features may support targeted mapping strategies ref [43]. At the same time, ablation simulations indicate that lesion efficacy depends not only on hitting a putative driver site, but on lesion geometry, continuity, and relation to boundaries or slow-conducting channels. Localized lesions may terminate AF by creating excitable gaps vulnerable to invading waves, by dislodging anchored reentry, or by connecting rotor cores to anatomical obstacles; conversely, incomplete or poorly placed lesions can stabilize organized atrial tachycardia ref [18], ref [20].

Model-guided comparisons of lesion sets further suggest that conventional PVI-plus-lines strategies may fail when drivers are extra-PV, whereas phase-singularity-guided circles, perforated circles, lines, or crosses placed over high-density driver regions can be more effective in specific substrates ref [9], ref [18], ref [20]. More aggressive streamline-based lesion sets may terminate persistent AF in simulation, but at the cost of greater tissue burden ref [9]. Overall, in silico studies emphasize that electrogram interpretation and ablation success are inseparable from mapping resolution, signal processing assumptions, and lesion design, all of which are highly relevant when relating simulated AF drivers to beat-to-beat atrial activation and ultimately to surface P-wave variability during sinus rhythm ref [39], ref [41], ref [9], ref [12].

subsections.section_title: Electrophysiological Mechanisms and Multiscale Atrial Modeling
subsections.subsection_title: Atrial Fibrillation Mechanisms, Remodeling, and Pharmacological Modulation
subsections.content:
In silico studies have clarified that AF initiation and maintenance emerge from a dynamic interplay among triggers, restitution, conduction delay, and substrate vulnerability. Simplified cellular automata as well as biophysical atrial models reproduce stochastic onset and spontaneous termination, showing that fibrosis burden, pulmonary-vein bursting, and restitution steepness interact nonlinearly rather than monotonically to determine AF probability ref [46]. Complementary clinical-computational work further identified steep repolarization restitution and reduced activation latency as convergent proarrhythmic pathways for AF initiation under adrenergic stimulation or rapid pacing, whereas adenosine shortened APD without facilitating AF because activation latency remained limiting ref [52].

Atrial remodeling and patient-specific modulators strongly shape these mechanisms and alter drug response. Pharmacological remodeling induced by chronic β-blocker therapy prolongs APD and ERP, suppresses alternans, reduces maximum capture rate, and shortens re-entry lifespan in multiscale human atrial simulations, supporting an anti-fibrillatory effect beyond acute autonomic blockade ref [51]. At the same time, transcriptional remodeling is increasingly modeled: reduced PITX2 expression depolarizes atrial resting membrane potential and enhances the efficacy of sodium-channel blockers by increasing post-repolarization refractoriness, thereby offering a mechanistic basis for genotype-informed antiarrhythmic selection ref [11]. Local parasympathetic heterogeneity is likewise important, because spatially distributed acetylcholine increases AF inducibility, while ganglionated plexi stimulation can generate pulmonary-vein triggers and local re-entry, linking autonomic remodeling to beat-to-beat atrial instability ref [19], ref [20].

Pharmacological modulation studies also highlight mechanism-specific termination pathways. Two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations suggest that agents targeting IK1, IKACh, or Na channels can destabilize rotors without necessarily increasing classical wavelength. Chloroquine terminates rotors more readily in paroxysmal than chronic AF substrates, implying reduced efficacy after electrical remodeling ref [12]. Rapidly unbinding Na-channel blockers terminate AF by reducing source current, enlarging rotor meander, and suppressing secondary wavebreaks rather than by simple wavelength prolongation ref [17]. Together, these studies indicate that AF behavior in sinus rhythm and under provocation depends not only on structural substrate, but also on remodeling state, autonomic tone, and drug- and genotype-dependent ionic context ref [51], ref [52], ref [11], ref [17].

subsections.section_title: Implications for ECG, P-Wave Morphology, and Computational Inference
subsections.content:
P-wave morphology during sinus rhythm emerges from the interaction of three principal determinants: the site of impulse initiation in the right atrial pacemaker complex, the route and timing of interatrial conduction, and atrial geometry/remodeling that shapes activation vectors and completion time of depolarization ref [4]. Contemporary anatomical and physiological data further indicate that the sinoatrial node is not a point source but an extended, heterogeneous pacemaker region with superior–inferior variability and paranodal extensions, providing a structural basis for wandering pacemaker behavior and spontaneous P-wave changes even in otherwise normal rhythm ref [55].

A key mechanistic insight from mapping and simulation studies is that modest shifts in the earliest right atrial activation site can substantially alter the initial right atrial vector and the terminal left atrial component of the P wave. When excitation originates more superiorly or anteriorly, activation more often reaches the left atrium through Bachmann’s bundle; more inferior or mid-septal origins favor posterior or inferior interatrial connections, thereby changing the left atrial breakthrough site and the polarity or magnitude of terminal deflections, especially in lead V1 ref [4], ref [54]. In personalized in silico atrial models, adjacent earliest activation sites produced up to a two-fold change in P-wave terminal force, independent of left atrial size, underscoring that abnormal terminal negativity cannot be interpreted purely as a surrogate of chamber enlargement ref [54].

These observations help explain beat-to-beat and patient-specific P-wave variability in AF-prone individuals during sinus rhythm. Structural remodeling, particularly fibrosis affecting thin posterior interatrial fibers, can suppress posterior breakthroughs and shift left atrial activation toward Bachmann-dominant pathways, accentuating biphasic or more negative terminal components without requiring marked global P-wave prolongation ref [4]. Thus, mechanistic interpretation of P-wave morphology should integrate pacemaker shift, interatrial connection integrity, and atrial structural substrate rather than rely on duration or terminal force alone ref [4], ref [54], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Implications for ECG, P-Wave Morphology, and Computational Inference
subsections.content:
Predictive and personalized computational inference seeks to invert the usual simulation workflow: rather than merely reproducing atrial activation, models are tuned with patient-specific anatomy, fibrosis, conduction, and rhythm data to infer latent substrate properties and forecast therapy response. Early clinical pipelines demonstrated that personalization of atrial geometry, rule-based fibers, interatrial connections, and conduction velocity could reproduce measured P-wave duration, left-atrial activation timing, and body-surface ECG features, thereby establishing a mechanistic bridge between sinus-rhythm observables and individualized atrial substrate characterization ref [11]. Such frameworks are especially relevant for AF patients in sinus rhythm, where beat-to-beat or subject-specific P-wave variation may reflect hidden heterogeneity in conduction pathways, remodeling state, and scar distribution rather than simple measurement noise ref [11].

A major advance has been the use of LGE-MRI-derived, patient-specific atrial models to identify arrhythmogenic regions and tailor ablation strategies. Editorial syntheses and cohort studies have argued that bi-atrial models reconstructed from each patient’s anatomy and fibrosis pattern can localize re-entrant driver–prone regions, test virtual lesion sets, and iteratively reveal emergent post-ablation substrates before the procedure is performed ref [3]. In this context, computational inference becomes predictive when model outputs are compared against clinical mapping or recurrence patterns, and personalized when inferred targets depend on the individual spatial organization of fibrosis rather than on generic lesion templates ref [3]. These developments also underscore a practical message for ECG-oriented research: noninvasive P-wave descriptors, when combined with imaging-informed digital twins, may provide priors for substrate inference and for selecting which patients are most likely to benefit from further invasive mapping or tailored ablation planning ref [11], ref [3].

Despite this promise, translation remains limited by uncertainty in fibrosis segmentation, fiber assignment, electrophysiological parameter identifiability, and the computational burden of running sufficiently rich stimulation protocols. Current opinion therefore emphasizes modular personalization pipelines, multi-source validation, and clinically compatible turnaround times rather than fully autonomous decision support ref [3]. For the present review topic, the key implication is that sinus-rhythm P-wave morphology should increasingly be viewed not only as a descriptive biomarker, but as an input to Bayesian or mechanistic inference frameworks that estimate patient-specific atrial properties and prospectively test intervention scenarios in silico ref [11], ref [3].

subsections.section_title: Implications for ECG, P-Wave Morphology, and Computational Inference
subsections.subsection_title: Simulation and Forward Modeling of Atrial ECG Signatures
subsections.content:
Simulation and forward modeling provide the mechanistic bridge between atrial depolarization and the surface P-wave, but this bridge remains sensitive to assumptions about geometry, tissue conductivities, and source representation. In electrocardiography, the forward problem is mathematically well posed yet not fully “solved” in practice, because realistic torso anatomy, inhomogeneous conductivities, and measurement-registration errors still materially affect body-surface potentials ref [2]. For atrial applications, multi-scale frameworks that couple detailed atrial activation to torso conduction have therefore become essential for interpreting how beat-to-beat shifts in sinus activation, interatrial conduction, or regional atrial substrate remodeling are expressed as changes in P-wave amplitude, polarity, and duration ref [3].

A key advance has been the construction of anatomically and electrophysiologically detailed atria–torso models that embed preferential bundles, regional ionic heterogeneity, and fiber architecture within realistic volume conductors ref [3]. These models show that P-wave morphology is jointly determined by intra-atrial activation sequence and by filtering through the torso, with anisotropy and organ-specific conductivities modulating both duration and waveform shape ref [3]. Importantly, explicit forward validation studies have demonstrated that homogeneous torso models can preserve gross map correlations yet still mislocalize extrema and distort the spatial gradients of body-surface potentials; inclusion of lungs, skeletal muscle anisotropy, and subcutaneous fat reduces, but does not abolish, these discrepancies ref [2]. This is particularly relevant for atrial signals, whose lower amplitudes make subtle modeling errors proportionally more consequential for P-wave interpretation.

For sinus-rhythm studies in AF populations, forward simulations are therefore valuable not only for reproducing canonical atrial ECG signatures, but also for decomposing which atrial regions dominate specific phases of the P-wave and for identifying body-surface locations with the highest sensitivity to atrial activity ref [3]. Such models support virtual experiments that are difficult or impossible in vivo, including isolation of region-specific contributions, comparison of isotropic versus anisotropic propagation, and testing how modest changes in conduction or source location could generate beat-to-beat P-wave variability ref [3]. At the same time, the lessons from forward-model validation caution against overinterpreting surface morphology without accounting for uncertainties in torso properties and source-to-surface transfer, especially when these simulations are later used as the basis for inverse or inference pipelines ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Implications for ECG, P-Wave Morphology, and Computational Inference
subsections.subsection_title: ECG-Based Inference of Atrial Fibrillation Sources and Dynamics
subsections.content:
Computational studies and inverse ECG mapping have made it increasingly plausible that atrial fibrillation (AF) source properties can be inferred noninvasively from body-surface recordings, provided the target is defined in spectral rather than purely spatiotemporal terms. Early biophysical simulations showed that surface ECG spectra reflect underlying atrial firing-rate organization, but also that reliance on a single dominant frequency (DF) or a single lead can mask multi-source dynamics; full multilead spectral structure better captures AF complexity and transitions between competing drivers ref [57]. This insight is consistent with experimental and clinical work linking AF maintenance to hierarchically organized high-frequency regions and interatrial DF gradients.

A key advance was the inverse reconstruction of atrial DF maps from body-surface potentials. In combined simulation–patient studies, noninvasive estimation of epicardial high-frequency regions reproduced left-to-right and right-to-left atrial DF gradients with substantially lower error in the frequency domain than in voltage or phase, supporting the view that inverse solutions preserve dominant spectral content more robustly than instantaneous activation patterns ref [59]. Related clinical-computational analyses further indicated that body-surface and inverse mapping can localize putative AF drivers or rotor-containing regions, but that spatial smoothing, regularization, and noise can simplify or distort phase maps even when driver-related frequency signatures remain detectable ref [4].

For surveying beat-to-beat atrial signatures during sinus rhythm, these AF-focused studies are important because they define the broader inverse problem: ECG observables are indirect, filtered projections of atrial dynamics, and not all latent features are equally inferable. In practice, frequency-based descriptors appear more stable for source localization than morphology-based instantaneous maps during AF ref [57], ref [59], while mechanistic validation against simulations and intracardiac recordings remains essential before translating inferred driver maps into individualized procedural guidance ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Implications for ECG, P-Wave Morphology, and Computational Inference
subsections.subsection_title: P-Wave Remodeling as a Marker of Ablation Response
subsections.content:
P-wave remodeling after ablation is increasingly viewed as a noninvasive marker of lesion effectiveness rather than a purely descriptive ECG change. Clinical studies of pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) consistently suggest that successful elimination of pulmonary vein-left atrial conduction is often accompanied by shortening of P-wave duration, whereas absent shortening, or even prolongation, is more common when reconnection and arrhythmia recurrence occur ref [6]. In the seminal study by Ogawa et al., maximal and filtered P-wave duration decreased significantly only in patients without recurrence, supporting the concept that acute post-ablation P-wave shortening reflects effective electrical exclusion of late-activating pulmonary vein sleeve tissue ref [6].

Mechanistically, this interpretation has been reinforced by simulation work showing that post-PVI P-wave remodeling is not determined solely by total atrial activation time. In computer models, PVI may slightly prolong biatrial activation because conduction is redirected around ablation lines, yet still shorten P-wave duration in selected precordial leads by eliminating low-amplitude terminal components arising from the pulmonary vein region ref [60]. The same study further showed that the magnitude and direction of apparent remodeling depend on ablation geometry, the extent of isolated atrial tissue, added roof lines, and the detection method used for P-wave offset, helping explain why clinical reports sometimes disagree on whether P-wave duration shortens or lengthens after ablation ref [60].

These findings have two implications for computational inference. First, P-wave remodeling should be interpreted as a lead-specific and method-dependent signature of altered atrial source distribution, not merely as a surrogate of global conduction slowing or acceleration ref [6], ref [60]. Second, simulation-guided analysis suggests that persistent or reversing post-ablation changes, especially in leads such as V3, V4, and posterior leads, may help identify pulmonary vein reconnection and stratify likelihood of recurrence during follow-up ref [60]. Accordingly, within sinus rhythm ECG analysis, post-ablation P-wave remodeling represents a promising bridge between procedural lesion assessment and personalized noninvasive monitoring of ablation response ref [6], ref [60].
